content: The WHO Steering Group utilized evidence profiles to summarize the effects of interventions on pre-specified outcomes. These profiles, along with GRADE tables and other relevant documents assessing values, preferences, resource requirements, cost-effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility, and equity, were shared with meeting participants in advance. Participants were invited to submit comments electronically before the meeting. Members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and other participants attended an online meeting organized by the Steering Group to discuss 11 WHO recommendations on labor induction at or beyond term. During the meeting, GDG members reviewed and deliberated on the balance between the desirable and undesirable effects of the intervention, the certainty of the supporting evidence, stakeholder values and preferences, resource implications, cost-effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility, and equity. These discussions informed the finalization of the recommendations and accompanying remarks. In accordance with WHO regulations, all experts involved in the guideline development process were required to declare any relevant interests before participating. GDG members completed a standard WHO Declaration of Interest (DOI) form, which was reviewed by the Steering Group. If conflicts of interest were identified, the Steering Group assessed their severity and determined whether they could compromise the expert’s objectivity. Minor conflicts were disclosed at the beginning of the meeting, while significant conflicts were managed according to WHO guidelines. During the GDG meeting, evidence summaries were reviewed, and clarifications were sought. The GDG applied the GRADE evidence-to-decision framework to evaluate the balance of benefits and harms, the certainty of evidence, and additional criteria such as stakeholder values, resource implications, acceptability, feasibility, and equity. Evidence-to-decision tables were used to synthesize these considerations. Decisions were made by consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of participants, with no opposition expressed by GDG members. Before the meeting, the WHO Steering Group prepared draft GRADE evidence profiles, evidence summaries, and other relevant documents, which were shared with participants two weeks in advance for comments. These documents were revised during the meeting based on participants’ deliberations. After the meeting, the Steering Group drafted a recommendation document reflecting the discussions and decisions, which was sent to GDG members and an External Review Group for final review and approval. The recommendations included the following: 1. Labor induction is recommended for women who are confirmed to have reached 41 weeks of gestation (conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence). This recommendation does not apply in settings where gestational age cannot be reliably estimated. Women should be informed about the potential need for labor induction, allowing them to ask questions and understand the benefits and risks. 2. Labor induction is not recommended for women with uncomplicated pregnancies at less than 41 weeks of gestation. The dissemination and implementation of these recommendations require collaboration among stakeholders at international, national, and local levels. Efforts should focus on increasing access to high-quality maternal care and integrating these recommendations into antenatal and intrapartum care programs. A shorter document summarizing the recommendations, remarks, implementation considerations, and research priorities will be made publicly available, along with annexes containing detailed methods, evidence-to-decision frameworks, and GRADE tables. The recommendations will be disseminated through WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, collaborating centers, and other relevant entities. They will also be available on the WHO website and in the WHO Reproductive Health Library. Updated recommendations will be shared during scientific conferences and translated into six UN languages for broader accessibility. Successful implementation depends on well-planned, participatory processes for adapting the recommendations to local contexts. This may involve revising national guidelines, ensuring the availability of necessary resources (e.g., induction agents and monitoring capacity), and fostering behavior change among healthcare providers. Local professional societies should play a key role in this process, and discussions with women during antenatal care should address the potential need for labor induction at ≥41 weeks. The GDG identified several research priorities to address knowledge gaps, including the risks of labor induction compared to elective cesarean section, the role of cesarean section in cases of failed induction, and policies for labor induction in settings with unreliable gestational age determination. Implementation should be monitored through clinical audits and other quality improvement efforts. Clear review criteria and indicators should be established, aligned with WHO standards for maternal and newborn care. The WHO Executive Guideline Steering Group will review and prioritize recommendations annually, updating them as new evidence emerges. Feedback and suggestions for additional questions are welcomed to ensure the recommendations remain relevant and evidence-based.
